How we see what cells actually look like — the five light-microscopy techniques, transmission and scanning electron microscopy, and the fixation → embedding → sectioning → staining pipeline that turns living tissue into a viewable specimen.

blocks.x: Key definitions

Resolution (resolving power)
The smallest distance between two points at which they can still be seen as separate. It is the true limiting factor of microscopy — magnification without adequate resolution just produces a bigger, blurrier image.

Contrast
The visible difference between a specimen and its background (or between parts of a specimen). Most light-microscopy techniques exist to generate contrast in specimens that are otherwise transparent and colourless.

Fixation
The rapid killing and preservation of tissue in a state as close as possible to living, functioning tissue — the essential first step of all histological work, preventing autolysis and decay.

Fluorescence
The absorption of light at a shorter wavelength (e.g. UV) followed by the near-instantaneous re-emission of light at a longer, visible wavelength.
Light Microscopy Techniques→ Electron Microscopy (TEM & SEM)→ Fixation & Embedding→ Sectioning & Staining
Generating contrast with visible light
Five ways of illuminating a specimen with visible (or near-visible) light, each solving the same basic problem: most biological material is transparent and colourless, so contrast has to be created.
Brightfield microscopy

Brightfield microscopy The standard, simplest and most widely used light-microscopy technique. Light from the substage condenser is gathered and shaped into a cone that is focused at the specimen plane. The specimen appears dark against a bright background. Because most unstained, transparent biological specimens produce very little inherent contrast, staining is required to make cellular detail visible.
Darkfield microscopy

Darkfield microscopy An opaque disc in the condenser blocks the direct light path, so the specimen is illuminated only by light scattered at an angle. The background appears dark, while the specimen appears bright/illuminated against it — the reverse of brightfield.

items: ✓Well suited to unstained, live or transparent specimens that are difficult to see in brightfield — e.g. spirochaete bacteria, or yeast cells suspended in liquid.
✓Can detect particles well below the normal diffraction limit (e.g. 40 nm gold particles) because scattered light from even a tiny particle is visible against a dark background.
✗Not well suited to viewing large objects — strong scattering from bulky structures floods the field and washes out detail.

blocks.x: Phase-contrast microscopy

Phase-contrast microscopy Exploits small differences in the refractive index within an otherwise transparent specimen to produce contrast without any staining. Light passing through denser regions of the specimen (organelles, membranes) is slightly shifted in phase relative to light passing through the surrounding medium — a shift the human eye cannot detect directly.

items: 1A special annulus (ring-shaped aperture) positioned below the stage shapes the illuminating light into a hollow cone.
2A matching phase plate built into the objective lens converts the resulting phase differences into visible differences in brightness — bright or dark contrast — that the eye can see.

3Especially valuable for observing live, unstained cells and their internal structures — cell movement, nuclei, and cytoplasmic flow — often combined with time-lapse photography to record dynamic cellular events over time.

blocks.x: Ultraviolet (UV) microscopy

UV microscopy Uses ultraviolet light — a shorter wavelength than visible light — to improve resolution roughly two-fold beyond what an equivalent visible-light microscope can achieve (resolution improves as wavelength decreases).

items: ✗Ordinary glass optics absorb UV light, so UV microscopes require special, expensive quartz lenses that are transparent to UV.
✗UV light is invisible to the human eye and can damage it, so the image cannot be viewed directly through an eyepiece — it must be captured by a camera or projected onto a fluorescent screen.

blocks.x: Fluorescence microscopy (UV-fluorescence)

Fluorescence Certain specimens are naturally auto-fluorescent, or can be labelled with a fluorochrome (fluorescent dye, e.g. fluorescein). When illuminated with UV or other short-wavelength light, the fluorochrome absorbs that light and almost instantly re-emits it at a longer, visible wavelength — the emitted light is what is imaged.

items: ✓Immunofluorescence: antibodies are chemically complexed to fluorescein and used to bind and visualise specific cellular proteins with high specificity.

✓Epifluorescence: both the exciting (UV) light and the longer-wavelength emitted light travel through the same objective lens; a dichroic mirror separates the two, reflecting the excitation light onto the specimen while allowing the emitted light through to the detector/eyepiece.

blocks.title: Quick recap — matching technique to purpose

items: Brightfield — routine, stained specimens; dark specimen on bright background.
Darkfield — unstained/live specimens, sub-diffraction particles; bright specimen on dark background.
Phase-contrast — live, unstained cells; converts refractive-index differences into brightness contrast.
UV microscopy — improved resolution via shorter wavelength; needs quartz optics, imaged indirectly.
Fluorescence — specific labelling of molecules (e.g. immunofluorescence) via fluorochromes that re-emit at longer wavelengths.

blocks.x: Beyond the limits of visible light
Electrons behave as waves with a far shorter wavelength than visible light, which is the fundamental reason electron microscopes can resolve far finer detail than any light microscope.

Why electrons give higher resolution Electrons have wave-like properties, with wavelength λ = √(1.5/V) nm, where V is the accelerating voltage. At 60 kV, λ ≈ 0.005 nm — theoretically a huge resolution gain over light microscopy. In practice, however, resolving power is limited not by wavelength alone but by weak specimen contrast and by imperfections in the electromagnetic lenses used to focus the beam.
Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM)
Electrons pass through the specimen

items: 1A beam of electrons emitted from a pin-shaped cathode is accelerated (typically 50–150 kV) and passed through an ultrathin section of the specimen.

2Electrons are deflected in proportion to the electron density / atomic mass of the material they pass through. Because biological specimens are made mostly of low-atomic-number elements (C, H, N, O), they naturally produce weak contrast — which is why heavy-metal staining is essential.
3Requires a vacuum, an extremely thin specimen section (50–100 nm), and heavy-metal staining for contrast. The image forms on a fluorescent screen or photographic/digital detector.
4Modern TEMs achieve a resolution of 0.2–0.3 nm, with useful magnification up to roughly 300,000×.

blocks.x: Scanning Electron Microscope (SEM)
Electrons scan the surface

items: 1Uses electrons, rather than light, to image the surface of a solid specimen — the beam is scanned across the surface rather than transmitted through it.
2Produces images with a large depth of field, giving the characteristic, attractive 3-D-looking appearance SEM images are known for.
3Standard SEM resolution is around 10 nm (finer with a field-emission SEM, FESEM), with magnification up to roughly 100,000–300,000×, compared with only around 2,000× for light microscopy.
4Widely used beyond biology too — e.g. examining fractured metal components, foreign particles, polymers, and electronic components, alongside biological surface samples.

blocks.x: Light microscope vs. electron microscope

c: Electrons, ~4 nm equivalent wavelength (image is monochrome)

blocks.title: Why TEM and SEM images look so different

items: TEM transmits electrons through an ultrathin slice — it reveals internal structure (organelles, membranes) as a flat, 2-D projection.
SEM scans electrons across a solid surface and detects those bounced back — it reveals external topography with a 3-D, textured appearance.
Both need a vacuum and cannot image living, wet tissue directly — hence the elaborate fixation/dehydration steps covered next.

blocks.x: Specimen preparation, stage 1 & 2
Before any tissue can be sectioned and stained, it must be killed, preserved and mechanically supported — the difference between a usable slide and a smear of decayed cells.

Fixation The rapid killing and preservation of tissue. Correct fixation is fundamental to all histological work — it prevents autolysis (self-digestion by the cell's own enzymes), bacterial or fungal attack, and structural damage from later processing steps.
Physical fixation

items: 1The specimen is immersed in liquid nitrogen (an inert cryogenic fluid at −196°C / −320°F), freezing it rapidly enough to prevent ice-crystal formation that would otherwise distort or rupture cellular structure.
2Frozen tissue stays fixed only while it remains frozen — for a permanent preparation, it must still undergo chemical fixation afterward.

blocks.x: Chemical fixation

Chemical fixatives Chemicals that stabilise proteins and lipids, the major structural components of the cell. For electron microscopy, fixatives must not form precipitates that would obscure fine organelle structure.

c: Acetic acid, alcohol, acetone, mercuric chloride, chromic acid, formaldehyde
Fix membrane lipids; osmium also adds electron density

blocks.x: Embedding

Why embedding is necessary Electron microscopy requires a high vacuum, so water must first be removed (dehydrated) from the specimen. The tissue is then infiltrated with a hard support medium so it can be cut into extremely thin, uniform sections.

items: 1Dehydration: the specimen is passed through a series of ethanol-water mixtures of increasing concentration, up to 100% alcohol, gradually replacing water with alcohol without distorting the tissue.
2Clearing: a wax solvent such as xylene replaces the alcohol, since alcohol and molten wax/resin are not directly miscible.
3Infiltration (light microscopy): xylene is replaced with molten paraffin wax, which then hardens around the tissue.

4Infiltration (electron microscopy): dehydration continues through a resin solvent — propylene oxide — then the tissue is infiltrated with a resin (e.g. epoxy resin), which is baked/polymerised in an oven to form a hard block.

blocks.x: Choosing the embedding medium Section thickness matters: too thick a section causes poor contrast from excessive electron scattering, so ultra-thin (~50 nm) sections are needed for EM. Paraffin wax supports thicker sections for light microscopy; epoxy resin/araldite supports ultra-thin EM sections; and soft plant material can be temporarily embedded in raw carrot or pawpaw as a cutting support when preparing thicker sections.
Example dehydration & embedding protocol (light microscopy, paraffin)
Fixation→ Dehydration→ Clearing→ Embedding
Specimen preparation, stage 3 & 4
The embedded block is cut into slices thin enough to be seen through, and then stained, since most thin sections are otherwise nearly transparent.
Sectioning

Microtome The instrument used to cut thin sections. It consists of a specimen holder, a sharp cutting edge, and a thickness-regulating mechanism. The cutting edge is a steel razor for wax-embedded (light microscopy) specimens, or a glass or diamond knife (ultramicrotome) for araldite/resin-embedded (EM) specimens. Frozen specimens are cut with a microtome housed in a freezer, typically around −20°C.
Staining

Why staining is needed
Thin sections are usually near-transparent under either light or electrons, so a staining step is required before the specimen can be properly examined.
Basic vs. acidic stains

Basic stains (cationic) Positively charged dyes that bind to negatively charged molecules such as nucleic acids. Examples: haematoxylin (stains the nucleus blue/purple), Crystal Violet, Methylene Blue, Safranin, basic fuchsin.

Acidic stains (anionic) Negatively charged (in acidic solution) dyes that bind to basic groups in the cytoplasm. Examples: eosin (stains the cytoplasm red/pink), Nigrosine, Picric acid, Acid fuchsin, India ink.

Haematoxylin & Eosin (H&E)
The classic, routine combined stain for animal tissue histology: haematoxylin marks the nucleus blue/purple while eosin marks the cytoplasm and extracellular material red/pink, giving good overall contrast between the two compartments.
Positive vs. negative staining

EM stains generate electron density, not colour Because the final image depends on an electron beam rather than light, EM stains must impart electron density/contrast, not colour. Heavy elements — lead (Pb) and uranium — increase electron density. Uranium binds nucleic acids and proteins; lead binds lipids/membranes; osmium (from fixation) also adds density to membranes, lipids and nucleic acids.

Positive staining Heavy-metal stains bind directly to structures — used for isolated organelles, membranes, viruses and ribosomes. The combined uranium + lead double-stain technique is the EM equivalent of H&E staining in light microscopy.

Negative staining An electron-dense stain (e.g. potassium phosphotungstate, uranyl acetate, ammonium molybdate) surrounds but does not bind the specimen, producing a dark background with the specimen appearing bright against it — commonly used for imaging viruses and other small particles.
Fixation→ Embedding→ Sectioning→ Staining

items: Basic (light micro) — cationic, binds nucleic acids, e.g. haematoxylin (nucleus).
Acidic (light micro) — anionic, binds cytoplasmic basic groups, e.g. eosin (cytoplasm).
Positive (EM) — heavy metal binds directly to the structure; e.g. uranium + lead double stain.
Negative (EM) — heavy-metal stain surrounds but doesn't bind the specimen; used for viruses/small particles.
